short_definition: A deepfake is AI-generated or AI-altered audio, video or imagery that convincingly imitates a real person's face, voice or actions, often without their consent.
explanation: Deepfakes are made with generative AI models that learn a person's face or voice from existing photos, videos or audio. The models then produce new content, such as face swaps, lip-synced video or cloned voices. The tools keep getting easier to use, and a convincing voice clone can sometimes be made from a short recording.

Deepfakes power scams and abuse. Examples include fake calls from a 'relative' in trouble, a 'CEO' demanding an urgent payment, celebrity videos promoting fake investment or crypto schemes, and non-consensual or misleading images. The same technology also has legitimate uses with consent, such as film dubbing and accessibility tools.

Detection tools are unreliable, and even careful people can be fooled by a good fake, so verifying requests works better than trying to spot fakes. Confirm urgent requests through a separate, known channel, agree on a family code word and be suspicious of pressure and secrecy. Report suspected fraud to your bank and local authorities. Laws on deepfakes differ by country.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): A finance assistant gets a video call that appears to show her CEO urgently requesting an $18,000 transfer to a new supplier. Following company policy, she hangs up and calls the CEO back on the number in the staff directory. The CEO knows nothing about it. The two-minute check stops the payment.
common_mistake: Treating a familiar face or voice as proof of identity. Verify any urgent request for money or data through a separate, known channel, however real the call looks.
title: Deepfake
